questions.explanation: PrEP requires confirmed HIV-negative status before initiation and regular retesting (typically every 3 months) to avoid resistance if acute HIV occurs. Renal function monitoring is required because of potential tenofovir nephrotoxicity. Hepatitis B screening is important because flares can occur with discontinuation. Adherence counseling is also critical.

questions.q: A school-age child with ADHD is prescribed methylphenidate. Which teaching point is most important for the parents?
options: “Give the medication in the evening to improve sleep.”
“Monitor growth, appetite, sleep, and heart rate; report significant appetite suppression or insomnia.”
“This medication has no potential for misuse.”
“It can be stopped abruptly without any effects once school performance improves.”
questions.explanation: Stimulant medications can suppress appetite, slow growth velocity, cause insomnia, and increase heart rate and blood pressure. Baseline and periodic monitoring of growth, vital signs, and sleep/appetite are recommended. Dosing is typically morning or early afternoon. Stimulants are controlled substances with misuse potential; abrupt cessation is usually not harmful but should be guided by the provider.

questions.q: A client with chronic angina refractory to other therapies is prescribed ranolazine. Which laboratory value or condition requires caution or dose adjustment?
options: Mild elevation of serum sodium
Significant hepatic impairment or concurrent strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
Well-controlled hypertension
History of remote seasonal allergies
questions.explanation: Ranolazine is contraindicated in significant hepatic impairment and requires dose limitation or avoidance with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., certain azoles, macrolides, protease inhibitors) because of increased exposure and QT prolongation risk. It has minimal effects on heart rate or blood pressure. QT monitoring may be considered in at-risk clients.

questions.q: A client receiving tobramycin for a serious gram-negative infection has a trough level drawn. Which result is most concerning?
options: Trough 0.8 mcg/mL (within or below typical target)
Trough 3.5 mcg/mL (elevated for most indications)
Peak level drawn correctly 30 minutes after infusion
Random level drawn during the infusion
questions.explanation: Aminoglycoside trough levels are monitored to minimize nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Elevated troughs (commonly >2 mcg/mL for traditional dosing, or per institutional protocol) indicate drug accumulation and increased toxicity risk. Dose adjustment or interval extension is usually required. Correct timing of peaks and troughs is essential for interpretation.

questions.q: A client with candidemia is prescribed caspofungin. Which statement about this medication is accurate?
options: “It requires extensive renal dose adjustment in all clients with CKD.”
“It is generally well tolerated; histamine-mediated infusion reactions can occur and are managed by slowing the infusion.”
“Oral bioavailability is high, so the IV form is rarely needed.”
“It has strong activity against most molds and is first-line for aspergillosis.”
questions.explanation: Echinocandins such as caspofungin are given only intravenously and are generally well tolerated. Infusion-related histamine reactions (rash, flushing, pruritus) can occur and are usually managed by slowing the rate. They have minimal renal clearance (little dose adjustment needed for CKD) and are first-line for many invasive Candida infections but have more limited mold coverage (anidulafungin/caspofungin are not first-line for most invasive aspergillosis).

questions.q: A client with schizophrenia is started on olanzapine. Which monitoring parameter is most important during the first months of therapy?
options: Serum sodium weekly
Weight, fasting glucose, and lipid profile
Complete blood count every 2 days
QT interval only at baseline
questions.explanation: Olanzapine (and other atypical antipsychotics, especially clozapine and olanzapine) carries a significant risk of metabolic syndrome, including weight gain, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia. Baseline and periodic monitoring of weight, waist circumference, fasting glucose, and lipids is recommended by current psychiatric and endocrine guidelines. Hematologic monitoring is more critical for clozapine; QT effects are less prominent with olanzapine than with some other agents.

questions.q: A client with major depressive disorder and chronic musculoskeletal pain is prescribed duloxetine. Which condition requires the nurse to  the order?
options: History of mild seasonal allergies
Uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma or substantial alcohol use
Well-controlled hypertension
History of remote childhood asthma
questions.explanation: Duloxetine (an SNRI) can increase the risk of mydriasis and is contraindicated or used with caution in uncontrolled narrow-angle glaucoma. It also carries a risk of hepatotoxicity and should be avoided in clients with substantial alcohol use or chronic liver disease. The other listed conditions are not primary contraindications.

questions.q: A client with an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection is prescribed nitrofurantoin. Which client factor is a contraindication to its use?
options: Mild intermittent asthma
Creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min
History of penicillin allergy
Occasional alcohol use
questions.explanation: Nitrofurantoin is ineffective and potentially toxic (increased risk of peripheral neuropathy and other adverse effects) when creatinine clearance is below approximately 30 mL/min because the drug does not reach adequate urinary concentrations and systemic exposure increases. It is commonly used for uncomplicated cystitis in clients with adequate renal function. Penicillin allergy and mild asthma are not contraindications.

questions.q: A client receiving rituximab for non-Hodgkin lymphoma develops fever, chills, and rigors 30 minutes into the first infusion. What is the nurse’s priority action?
options: Continue the infusion at the same rate and administer a PRN antipyretic
Stop or slow the infusion, notify the provider, and manage the infusion reaction according to protocol
Increase the infusion rate to complete it more quickly
Attribute the symptoms to anxiety and provide reassurance only
questions.explanation: Rituximab commonly causes infusion-related reactions, especially with the first dose. Standard management includes stopping or slowing the infusion, administering prescribed medications (acetaminophen, antihistamines, corticosteroids), and supporting the client. Severe reactions require permanent discontinuation and emergency measures. Premedication and graded infusion rates are routine preventive strategies.

questions.q: A client at 26 weeks gestation in preterm labor is considered for indomethacin tocolysis. Which assessment is most important before initiation?
options: Maternal serum sodium
Gestational age, fetal echocardiogram considerations, and amniotic fluid volume (risk of oligohydramnios and ductal constriction)
Maternal fasting glucose only
Maternal platelet count exclusively
questions.explanation: Indomethacin (an NSAID) used for tocolysis can cause premature closure or constriction of the fetal ductus arteriosus and oligohydramnios, with risk increasing at later gestational ages (generally avoided after 31–32 weeks). Fetal monitoring and assessment of amniotic fluid are important. Duration of use is typically limited. Maternal sodium and glucose are not the primary concerns for this indication.

questions.q: A high-risk infant is prescribed palivizumab. What is the primary purpose of this medication?
options: Treatment of acute respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) bronchiolitis
Prevention of serious RSV lower respiratory tract disease in high-risk infants and children
Stimulation of surfactant production in preterm infants
Routine vaccination against influenza
questions.explanation: Palivizumab is a monoclonal antibody given monthly during the RSV season to prevent severe RSV disease in high-risk infants (e.g., premature, chronic lung disease, certain congenital heart disease). It is not used for treatment of established infection, does not stimulate surfactant, and is not an influenza vaccine.

questions.q: A client with atrial fibrillation is prescribed dofetilide. Which action is essential during initiation?
options: Outpatient initiation with weekly follow-up only
Inpatient initiation with continuous cardiac monitoring and serial QT interval assessments
Administration without regard to renal function
Combination with other QT-prolonging drugs to enhance efficacy
questions.explanation: Dofetilide is a Class III antiarrhythmic with a significant risk of torsades de pointes. Guidelines require inpatient initiation with continuous ECG monitoring, serial creatinine clearance calculation, and QT assessment. Dose is strictly adjusted for renal function. Concomitant QT-prolonging drugs are generally avoided.

questions.q: A client who received a renal transplant is prescribed mycophenolate mofetil. Which teaching point is most important?
options: “This medication can be stopped once rejection risk decreases after 3 months.”
“Report any signs of infection, unusual bruising, or gastrointestinal intolerance; effective contraception is required.”
“Mycophenolate has no effect on the immune system.”
“Live vaccines are safe while taking this medication.”
questions.explanation: Mycophenolate is a potent immunosuppressant that increases infection and malignancy risk and can cause bone marrow suppression and GI toxicity. It is teratogenic; effective contraception is mandatory for persons of childbearing potential. Therapy is generally long-term. Live vaccines are contraindicated during significant immunosuppression.

questions.q: A client in the emergency department with severe acute agitation and psychosis is prescribed intramuscular ketamine. Which monitoring is essential after administration?
options: Serum sodium only
Continuous or frequent monitoring of airway, breathing, circulation, and level of sedation
Fasting glucose every 15 minutes
Daily weights
questions.explanation: Ketamine can cause sedation, emergence reactions, hypertension, tachycardia, and, at higher doses, respiratory depression. Close monitoring of vital signs, airway, and mental status is required until the client is recovered. It is increasingly used for acute agitation when other agents are ineffective or contraindicated.

questions.q: A client with severe hyperkalemia and ECG changes is prescribed sodium polystyrene sulfonate. Which statement about this medication is accurate?
options: “It works immediately to lower potassium within minutes.”
“It exchanges sodium for potassium in the gastrointestinal tract and takes several hours to have an effect; it is not first-line for life-threatening hyperkalemia with ECG changes.”
“It is given intravenously for rapid effect.”
“It has no risk of intestinal complications.”
questions.explanation: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) binds potassium in the gut and lowers serum potassium over hours. It is not appropriate as sole therapy for life-threatening hyperkalemia with ECG changes (where calcium, insulin/glucose, bicarbonate, or dialysis are used first). Rare but serious intestinal necrosis has been reported, especially with sorbitol formulations or in clients with bowel disease.

questions.q: A client prescribed metronidazole for a anaerobic infection reports plans to attend a wedding and drink wine. What is the most important teaching point?
options: “A small amount of wine is safe with this medication.”
“Avoid all alcohol during treatment and for at least 48–72 hours after the last dose because of the risk of a disulfiram-like reaction.”
“Alcohol will only reduce the effectiveness of the antibiotic.”
“You may drink alcohol if you take the metronidazole with food.”
questions.explanation: Metronidazole inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase and can cause a disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, hypotension) when combined with alcohol. Clients must avoid alcohol during therapy and for a period after completion (commonly 48–72 hours). This is a critical safety teaching point.

questions.q: A client receiving clindamycin develops frequent watery diarrhea and abdominal cramping. What is the nurse’s priority action?
options: Administer a PRN antidiarrheal and continue the antibiotic
Hold the clindamycin, isolate the client if appropriate, and notify the provider of possible Clostridioides difficile infection
Encourage yogurt intake and reassess in 24 hours
Increase the clindamycin dose to overcome resistance
questions.explanation: Clindamycin carries a high risk of Clostridioides difficile–associated diarrhea and colitis. New or worsening diarrhea requires holding the antibiotic, implementing contact precautions if indicated, obtaining a stool sample, and notifying the provider. Antimotility agents can worsen outcomes and should be avoided until C. difficile is excluded.

questions.q: A client with major depressive disorder is prescribed venlafaxine. Which monitoring parameter is most important during dose titration?
options: Serum sodium only
Blood pressure
Fasting lipid panel weekly
Complete blood count every 2 days
questions.explanation: Venlafaxine (an SNRI) can cause dose-dependent increases in blood pressure. Blood pressure should be monitored regularly, especially during initiation and titration. Hyponatremia can occur (particularly in older adults), but blood pressure elevation is a primary and common concern. Routine frequent CBCs or lipids are not the highest-priority parameters for this agent.

questions.q: A client with generalized anxiety disorder is prescribed buspirone. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding?
options: “This medication will provide immediate relief during a panic attack.”
“It may take 1–2 weeks or longer to feel the full effect, and it has a low risk of dependence.”
“I can safely drink alcohol while taking buspirone.”
“Buspirone is a benzodiazepine and should only be used short-term.”
questions.explanation: Buspirone is a non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic that lacks immediate effects, anticonvulsant properties, and significant dependence potential. Onset of anxiolytic action is typically delayed (1–2 weeks or more). Alcohol should be avoided because of additive CNS effects. It is not a benzodiazepine and is often used for longer-term management.

questions.q: A postpartum client with uterine atony is prescribed methylergonovine. Which condition is a contraindication to its use?
options: Mild postpartum hemorrhage controlled with fundal massage
Hypertension or preeclampsia
Multiparity
Breastfeeding intention
questions.explanation: Methylergonovine (an ergot alkaloid) causes potent vasoconstriction and is contraindicated in clients with hypertension, preeclampsia, or cardiovascular disease because it can precipitate severe hypertensive reactions or stroke. It is used for postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony after other measures. Breastfeeding is generally compatible once the acute dose is given.

questions.q: A newborn is to receive intramuscular vitamin K shortly after birth. What is the primary purpose of this medication?
options: Prevention of early- and late-onset vitamin K deficiency bleeding
Immediate treatment of neonatal jaundice
Stimulation of surfactant production
Prevention of group B streptococcal infection
questions.explanation: Newborns have low vitamin K stores and are at risk for vitamin K deficiency bleeding (including late-onset intracranial hemorrhage). A single intramuscular dose of vitamin K shortly after birth is standard prophylaxis recommended by major pediatric and public health guidelines. It does not treat jaundice, stimulate surfactant, or prevent GBS infection.

questions.q: A client receiving intravenous lidocaine for ventricular arrhythmias develops perioral numbness, tinnitus, and confusion. What is the nurse’s priority action?
options: Continue the infusion and reassess in 15 minutes
Stop the infusion and notify the provider of possible lidocaine toxicity
Increase the infusion rate to achieve therapeutic levels faster
Administer a fluid bolus and continue monitoring
questions.explanation: Early signs of lidocaine toxicity include circumoral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, and CNS changes (confusion, seizures). The infusion must be stopped immediately and the provider notified. Continued administration can progress to seizures or cardiac arrest. Lidocaine is a high-alert medication requiring careful dosing and monitoring.

questions.q: A client with atrial fibrillation is prescribed sotalol. Which assessment is essential before initiation and during dose titration?
options: Serum sodium only
QT interval measurement and continuous or frequent cardiac monitoring
Fasting blood glucose daily
Daily weights exclusively
questions.explanation: Sotalol has significant Class III antiarrhythmic activity and can prolong the QT interval, increasing the risk of torsades de pointes. Baseline and serial QT measurements, along with inpatient initiation or close monitoring for many clients, are recommended. Electrolyte balance (especially potassium and magnesium) is also critical. The other parameters are not the primary safety focus for sotalol.

questions.q: A client with heart failure and elevated heart rate is prescribed ivabradine. Which finding is a contraindication or reason to hold the medication?
options: Heart rate 75 bpm in sinus rhythm
Blood pressure 105/65 mm Hg
Atrial fibrillation or heart rate already below 60 bpm
Mild fatigue
questions.explanation: Ivabradine selectively inhibits the funny current (If) in the sinoatrial node and is indicated only for clients in sinus rhythm. It is contraindicated in atrial fibrillation and should be held or avoided if resting heart rate is already low (generally <60 bpm before initiation or <50 bpm on therapy). It has minimal effect on blood pressure.

questions.q: A client receiving paclitaxel for breast cancer develops flushing, wheezing, and hypotension during the infusion. What is the nurse’s priority action?
options: Slow the infusion rate and continue
Stop the infusion, notify the provider, and prepare to administer emergency medications for hypersensitivity
Administer a PRN antiemetic and reassess
Reassure the client that mild reactions are common and will pass
questions.explanation: Paclitaxel is associated with significant hypersensitivity reactions (related in part to the Cremophor vehicle). Premedication with corticosteroids, H1 and H2 blockers is standard. Any signs of anaphylaxis or severe reaction require immediate cessation of the infusion, supportive care, and emergency treatment. Mild reactions may sometimes be managed with rate reduction after evaluation, but the priority is to stop and assess.

questions.q: A client with type 2 diabetes and a history of heart failure is prescribed pioglitazone. What is the nurse’s primary concern?
options: Risk of significant weight loss
Fluid retention and exacerbation of heart failure
Severe hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy
Marked QT prolongation
questions.explanation: Thiazolidinediones (TZDs) such as pioglitazone cause fluid retention and can worsen or precipitate heart failure. They are contraindicated in clients with established New York Heart Association Class III or IV heart failure. Hypoglycemia risk is low when used alone; weight gain (not loss) is common. Cardiac monitoring and assessment for edema are essential.

questions.q: A client with type 2 diabetes is started on sitagliptin. Which teaching point is appropriate?
options: “This medication commonly causes severe hypoglycemia when used alone.”
“Report any severe joint pain or signs of pancreatitis (severe abdominal pain).”
“Sitagliptin must be taken with the first bite of each meal.”
“This drug class has no risk of immune-mediated reactions.”
questions.explanation: DPP-4 inhibitors carry rare risks of acute pancreatitis and severe joint pain (arthralgia). Clients should be taught to report these symptoms promptly. Hypoglycemia risk is low as monotherapy. Dosing is usually once daily without regard to meals (unlike some other agents). Hypersensitivity reactions, including rare severe skin reactions, can occur.

questions.q: A client with chronic pain is prescribed methadone. Which assessment is most important during initiation and dose titration?
options: Serum sodium only
QT interval monitoring and assessment for respiratory depression
Fasting lipid panel weekly
Daily weights exclusively
questions.explanation: Methadone can prolong the QT interval and increase the risk of torsades de pointes; baseline and follow-up ECGs are often recommended, especially at higher doses. It also has a long and variable half-life, increasing the risk of delayed respiratory depression during titration. Close monitoring of respiratory status and sedation is mandatory.

questions.q: A male client prescribed trazodone for insomnia reports a prolonged, painful erection lasting more than 4 hours. What is the nurse’s priority action?
options: Document the finding as a common side effect
Instruct the client to seek emergency care immediately for possible priapism
Administer a PRN analgesic and reassess in 2 hours
Reassure the client that the erection will resolve spontaneously
questions.explanation: Trazodone is associated with priapism, a urologic emergency that can lead to permanent erectile dysfunction if not treated promptly. Clients must be taught to seek immediate medical attention for an erection lasting longer than 4 hours. This is not a benign or self-limiting side effect.

questions.q: A client receiving bleomycin for lymphoma develops a dry cough and mild dyspnea. What is the nurse’s priority action?
options: Encourage increased fluid intake and continue the regimen
Hold the medication and notify the provider of possible pulmonary toxicity
Administer a PRN cough suppressant and reassess later
Attribute the symptoms to anxiety and provide reassurance
questions.explanation: Bleomycin is associated with dose-dependent pulmonary toxicity that can progress to irreversible fibrosis. New or worsening respiratory symptoms require immediate evaluation and usually discontinuation of the drug. Cumulative dose tracking and baseline/periodic pulmonary assessments are standard in oncology practice.

questions.q: A client at 30 weeks gestation in preterm labor is prescribed nifedipine. Which finding requires the nurse to hold the dose and notify the provider?
options: Blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg
Maternal heart rate 125 bpm and complaints of severe headache and flushing
Mild residual contractions
Fetal heart rate with moderate variability
questions.explanation: Nifedipine (a calcium-channel blocker used off-label for tocolysis) can cause significant maternal hypotension, reflex tachycardia, headache, and flushing. Severe maternal tachycardia or symptomatic hypotension warrants holding the dose and provider notification. Mild residual contractions and reassuring fetal status are expected or acceptable findings.

questions.q: A client with a history of seizures is prescribed meropenem for a serious infection. What is the nurse’s primary concern?
options: Reduced seizure threshold and increased risk of seizures
Severe hypoglycemia
Marked bradycardia
Significant weight gain
questions.explanation: Carbapenems (especially imipenem, and to a lesser extent meropenem) can lower the seizure threshold, particularly in clients with pre-existing CNS disorders, renal impairment, or high doses. Dose adjustment and seizure precautions are important. The other listed effects are not primary concerns with this class.

questions.q: A client with depression and insomnia is prescribed mirtazapine. Which teaching point is appropriate?
options: “This medication commonly causes significant weight loss and insomnia.”
“It may increase appetite and cause weight gain; take it at bedtime because it can cause sedation.”
“Mirtazapine has a high risk of sexual side effects compared with SSRIs.”
“You should take this medication in the morning to avoid drowsiness.”
questions.explanation: Mirtazapine frequently causes increased appetite, weight gain, and sedation (especially at lower doses). It is often dosed at bedtime. Sexual side effects are generally less prominent than with SSRIs. Clients should be monitored for weight changes and educated about the sedative effects.

questions.q: A client with variceal bleeding is prescribed octreotide. What is the primary purpose of this medication in this setting?
options: Long-term reduction of portal pressure through beta-blockade
Reduction of splanchnic blood flow and control of acute bleeding
Immediate reversal of anticoagulation
Stimulation of platelet production
questions.explanation: Octreotide (a somatostatin analog) reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure and is used in the acute management of variceal hemorrhage. It is not a substitute for endoscopic therapy or long-term beta-blockade for secondary prophylaxis. It does not reverse anticoagulation or stimulate platelets.

questions.q: A client with hypertensive emergency is receiving intravenous hydralazine. Which assessment finding requires the most immediate action?
options: Blood pressure decreased from 220/120 mm Hg to 170/100 mm Hg
New onset of chest pain and reflex tachycardia
Mild headache
Warm, flushed skin
questions.explanation: Hydralazine causes arterial vasodilation and can produce reflex tachycardia and increased myocardial oxygen demand, potentially precipitating angina or ischemia, especially in clients with coronary artery disease. A controlled blood pressure reduction is the goal; chest pain requires immediate evaluation. Mild headache and flushing are common side effects.

questions.q: A client with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is prescribed sacubitril/valsartan. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I must stop my ACE inhibitor at least 36 hours before starting this medication.”
“I should have my blood pressure, kidney function, and potassium checked regularly.”
“I can continue taking my lisinopril together with this new medication.”
“This medication can cause low blood pressure and high potassium.”
questions.explanation: Sacubitril/valsartan (an ARNI) cannot be combined with an ACE inhibitor because of the increased risk of angioedema and other adverse effects. A 36-hour washout period after the last ACE inhibitor dose is required before initiation. Blood pressure, renal function, and potassium monitoring are essential. Clients must understand these safety requirements.

questions.q: A client who received a coronary stent is prescribed ticagrelor. Which teaching point is most important?
options: “You may stop this medication after 30 days if you feel well.”
“Report any unusual bleeding or bruising; do not stop the medication without talking to your cardiologist.”
“This medication has no interaction with aspirin.”
“Ticagrelor is taken only once daily.”
questions.explanation: Dual antiplatelet therapy (usually aspirin + ticagrelor) is critical after stent placement to prevent stent thrombosis. Premature discontinuation significantly increases the risk of thrombotic events. Clients must report bleeding and never stop the drug without cardiology guidance. Ticagrelor is typically dosed twice daily and is used together with aspirin.

questions.q: A client with depression and a history of seizures is prescribed bupropion. What is the nurse’s primary concern?
options: Risk of weight gain
Lowered seizure threshold and increased risk of seizures
Severe bradycardia
Marked QT prolongation
questions.explanation: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold in a dose-dependent manner and is contraindicated in clients with current or prior seizure disorders, or conditions that increase seizure risk (e.g., abrupt alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, eating disorders). It is generally weight-neutral or associated with modest weight loss and does not typically cause significant bradycardia or QT prolongation.

questions.q: A client is prescribed a transdermal fentanyl patch for chronic cancer pain. Which instruction is essential?
options: “Apply the new patch to the same site each time for consistent absorption.”
“Avoid exposing the patch to heat (heating pads, hot baths, fever) because this can increase drug release.”
“Cut the patch in half if the dose is too strong.”
“Place used patches in the regular household trash without special precautions.”
questions.explanation: Heat increases the rate of fentanyl release from the patch and can cause overdose. Patches should be applied to a different site each time, never cut, and disposed of properly (fold adhesive sides together and follow local safe-disposal guidelines) because residual drug remains. These are critical high-alert medication safety points.

questions.q: A client with hepatic encephalopathy is prescribed lactulose. Which assessment finding indicates the medication is effective?
options: Increased blood ammonia level
Two to three soft stools per day and improved mental status
Hard, infrequent stools
Worsening confusion and asterixis
questions.explanation: Lactulose acidifies the colon, traps ammonia as ammonium, and promotes its excretion through osmotic diarrhea. The therapeutic goal is typically 2–3 soft stools daily along with improvement in mental status. Hard stools indicate inadequate effect; rising ammonia or worsening encephalopathy indicates treatment failure.

questions.q: A client with a high tumor burden is starting chemotherapy and is prescribed allopurinol. What is the primary purpose of this medication in this setting?
options: Prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea
Reduction of uric acid production to prevent tumor lysis syndrome complications
Stimulation of white blood cell recovery
Prevention of hemorrhagic cystitis
questions.explanation: Tumor lysis syndrome releases large amounts of purines that are metabolized to uric acid, which can cause acute kidney injury. Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase and reduces uric acid formation. Hydration and, in high-risk cases, rasburicase are also used. Allopurinol does not address nausea, neutrophil recovery, or hemorrhagic cystitis.

questions.q: A client at 28 weeks gestation with preterm labor is prescribed antenatal betamethasone. What is the primary purpose of this medication?
options: Immediate tocolysis to stop contractions
Acceleration of fetal lung maturity and reduction of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
Treatment of maternal infection
Prevention of maternal hypertension
questions.explanation: A course of antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone or dexamethasone) is given to clients at risk of preterm delivery to accelerate fetal lung maturation, reduce respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular hemorrhage, and neonatal mortality. It is not a tocolytic; separate agents are used for contraction suppression when indicated.

questions.q: A client receiving intravenous vancomycin has a trough level drawn. Which result would most likely require a dose adjustment?
options: Trough 8 mcg/mL (for a serious MRSA infection with target 15–20 mcg/mL)
Trough 18 mcg/mL (within target range)
Peak level of 25 mcg/mL
Random level drawn during infusion
questions.explanation: For serious infections (e.g., MRSA bacteremia, endocarditis, pneumonia), current guidelines prefer AUC-guided dosing (AUC/MIC 400–600); when troughs are used the historical target was 15–20 mcg/mL. A trough of 8 mcg/mL is subtherapeutic and would typically require a dose increase. Troughs are preferred over peaks for routine monitoring; levels must be timed correctly (just before the next dose).

questions.q: A client with type 2 diabetes is prescribed semaglutide. Which teaching point is most important?
options: “This medication is taken orally once daily with no special timing.”
“Start with a low dose and titrate slowly to reduce gastrointestinal side effects; report severe abdominal pain.”
“Hypoglycemia is very common when this drug is used alone.”
“This medication has no effect on weight.”
questions.explanation: GLP-1 receptor agonists commonly cause nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea; slow dose titration improves tolerability. Rare but serious risks include pancreatitis (severe abdominal pain must be reported) and, with some agents, gallbladder disease. They carry a low risk of hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy and typically promote weight loss. Injectable forms have specific administration schedules.

questions.q: A client with severe hypomagnesemia is prescribed intravenous magnesium sulfate. Which nursing action is essential?
options: Administer the dose by rapid IV push over 1–2 minutes
Infuse via a pump at a controlled rate and monitor deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output
Mix magnesium with calcium gluconate in the same bag
Continue the infusion even if the client develops absent deep tendon reflexes
questions.explanation: Intravenous magnesium is a high-alert medication. Rapid administration can cause hypotension, flushing, or cardiac arrest. Continuous or frequent monitoring of vital signs, deep tendon reflexes, respiratory status, and urine output is required. Absent reflexes or respiratory depression signals toxicity; calcium gluconate is the antidote and should be readily available. Magnesium and calcium are not mixed in the same solution for routine administration.

questions.q: A client who developed a persistent dry cough while taking lisinopril is switched to losartan. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding?
options: “I will no longer need to have my kidney function or potassium checked.”
“This medication can still cause high potassium and should not be taken with potassium supplements unless ordered.”
“Losartan is completely free of any risk of angioedema.”
“I can safely use salt substitutes that contain potassium while taking this drug.”
questions.explanation: Angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARBs) do not cause the bradykinin-mediated cough associated with ACE inhibitors, but they still carry a risk of hyperkalemia and reduced renal function. Periodic monitoring of potassium and creatinine remains necessary. Angioedema can still occur (although less frequently than with ACE inhibitors). Potassium-containing salt substitutes should be avoided unless specifically approved by the provider.

questions.q: A client with asthma is prescribed montelukast. Which teaching point is most important?
options: “Use this medication for immediate relief during an acute asthma attack.”
“Take this medication regularly as prescribed for prevention; it is not a rescue inhaler.”
“This medication can be stopped once symptoms improve for a few days.”
“Montelukast has no effect on mood or behavior.”
questions.explanation: Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist used for maintenance therapy and prevention of asthma symptoms or allergic rhinitis; it has no role in acute bronchospasm. Clients must continue to have a short-acting beta-agonist available for rescue. Neuropsychiatric events (mood changes, suicidal thoughts) have been reported and should be discussed. Therapy is ongoing rather than intermittent.

questions.q: A client is prescribed sucralfate for a duodenal ulcer. Which instruction is appropriate?
options: “Take the medication with meals and at bedtime for best effect.”
“Take sucralfate on an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before meals and at bedtime.”
“Crush the tablet and mix it with an antacid to improve absorption.”
“Sucralfate can be taken at the same time as other medications without spacing.”
questions.explanation: Sucralfate forms a protective barrier over the ulcer and requires an acidic environment for activation. It should be taken on an empty stomach, 1 hour before meals and at bedtime. Antacids and other medications should be spaced (usually by at least 30–60 minutes) because they can interfere with binding or absorption. Crushing is acceptable for some formulations but should not be mixed directly with antacids.

questions.q: A client of childbearing potential is prescribed misoprostol for prevention of NSAID-induced ulcers. Which assessment is essential before starting therapy?
options: Baseline serum sodium
Negative pregnancy test and effective contraception counseling
Fasting lipid profile
Complete blood count every 2 days
questions.explanation: Misoprostol is a prostaglandin analog that can cause uterine contractions and abortion. It is contraindicated in pregnancy (Category X for this indication). A negative pregnancy test and reliable contraception are mandatory before initiation. Clients must be fully informed of the abortifacient risk. Other laboratory tests are not the primary pre-treatment requirement.

questions.q: A client taking sertraline for depression is prescribed tramadol for acute pain. What is the nurse’s primary concern?
options: Reduced analgesic efficacy of tramadol
Increased risk of serotonin syndrome
Severe hypotension
Marked hyperglycemia
questions.explanation: Tramadol has serotonin- and norepinephrine-reuptake inhibiting properties. Combining it with SSRIs, SNRIs, or other serotonergic agents increases the risk of serotonin syndrome. Clients should be monitored for agitation, hyperthermia, autonomic changes, and neuromuscular findings. Alternative analgesics may be preferred when possible.

questions.q: A client with osteoporosis is prescribed denosumab. Which teaching point is essential?
options: “This medication is given as a daily oral tablet.”
“You will receive a subcutaneous injection every 6 months; calcium and vitamin D supplementation is usually required.”
“Denosumab has no risk of hypocalcemia.”
“You can stop the medication at any time without effects on bone density.”
questions.explanation: Denosumab is administered as a subcutaneous injection every 6 months. It can cause hypocalcemia, so adequate calcium and vitamin D intake (or supplementation) is required, and serum calcium should be checked before each dose. Discontinuation can lead to rebound bone loss and increased fracture risk; ongoing therapy or transition planning is important.

questions.q: A Rh-negative mother delivers an Rh-positive infant. When should Rho(D) immune globulin ideally be administered?
options: Only if the mother develops antibodies during the current pregnancy
Within 72 hours after delivery (and also at 28 weeks gestation prophylactically)
One week after delivery if the infant’s direct Coombs test is positive
Only in subsequent pregnancies
questions.explanation: Rho(D) immune globulin prevents maternal sensitization to Rh-positive fetal red cells. Standard guidelines recommend administration at approximately 28 weeks gestation and within 72 hours after delivery of an Rh-positive infant (or after any potentially sensitizing event). It is given to non-sensitized Rh-negative mothers regardless of the infant’s Coombs result.

questions.q: A client with a documented severe anaphylactic reaction to penicillin requires an antibiotic. Which statement is most accurate regarding cephalosporin use?
options: All cephalosporins are completely safe in clients with any penicillin allergy
Cross-reactivity exists; the risk is higher with first-generation cephalosporins and in clients with a history of severe IgE-mediated reactions
Cephalosporins are always preferred over alternative antibiotic classes
Skin testing is never required before giving a cephalosporin
questions.explanation: Cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is lower than historically believed but is not zero. Risk is higher with first-generation cephalosporins (similar side chains) and in clients with a history of anaphylaxis or other severe immediate reactions. Current guidelines recommend careful assessment, consideration of alternative agents, and, when appropriate, allergy consultation or graded challenge rather than automatic avoidance of the entire class.

questions.q: An 82-year-old client with type 2 diabetes is prescribed glyburide. Why should the nurse  this order?
options: Glyburide is the preferred sulfonylurea in older adults
Glyburide has a prolonged duration and active metabolites, increasing the risk of severe, prolonged hypoglycemia in older adults
Sulfonylureas have no risk of hypoglycemia
Glyburide does not require renal function assessment
questions.explanation: Glyburide is identified in the Beers Criteria as a potentially inappropriate medication for older adults because of its long half-life and active metabolites, which significantly raise the risk of prolonged hypoglycemia. Shorter-acting agents or alternative drug classes are generally preferred. Renal function and hypoglycemia risk must always be considered with sulfonylureas.

questions.q: A client with asthma is prescribed an inhaled corticosteroid. Which teaching point is essential?
options: “Use this inhaler only when you have acute symptoms.”
“Rinse your mouth with water and spit after each use to reduce the risk of oral candidiasis.”
“Inhaled corticosteroids have no systemic effects even at high doses.”
“You can stop the medication once your peak flow normalizes.”
questions.explanation: Inhaled corticosteroids can cause local side effects, including oral thrush and dysphonia. Rinsing the mouth (and using a spacer when appropriate) reduces this risk. These agents are controller medications and must be taken regularly. Systemic effects are possible at high doses or with prolonged use, and abrupt cessation can lead to loss of asthma control.

questions.q: A client with rheumatoid arthritis is prescribed adalimumab (a TNF inhibitor). Which assessment is essential before initiating therapy?
options: Baseline serum sodium
Screening for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B
Fasting lipid panel only
Daily weights for one week
questions.explanation: TNF inhibitors increase the risk of serious infections, including reactivation of latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B. Guidelines require screening for TB (and often hepatitis B/C) before starting therapy. Clients must also be taught to report signs of infection promptly. Serum sodium and routine lipids are not the primary pre-treatment requirements for this class.

questions.q: A client with rheumatoid arthritis is prescribed weekly methotrexate. Which teaching point is most important?
options: “Take the medication daily for best effect.”
“Avoid alcohol and report any signs of infection, unusual bleeding, or mouth sores.”
“This medication is safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding.”
“Folic acid supplements should never be taken with methotrexate.”
questions.explanation: Methotrexate is given once weekly (daily dosing can cause severe toxicity). It is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy. Alcohol increases hepatotoxicity risk. Bone marrow suppression, mucositis, and infection risk require prompt reporting of related symptoms. Folic acid is commonly co-prescribed to reduce adverse effects.

questions.q: A client receiving cyclophosphamide for lymphoma is instructed about supportive care. Which measure is most important to prevent a serious adverse effect?
options: Restrict fluid intake to reduce nausea
Maintain high oral or intravenous fluid intake and empty the bladder frequently
Avoid all antiemetics to prevent interactions
Take the medication only at bedtime
questions.explanation: Cyclophosphamide can cause hemorrhagic cystitis due to the toxic metabolite acrolein. Aggressive hydration and frequent voiding (sometimes with mesna) reduce contact time of the metabolite with the bladder mucosa. Fluid restriction would increase risk. Antiemetics are commonly used; timing is less critical than hydration.

questions.q: A client with herpes zoster is prescribed intravenous acyclovir. Which nursing action is essential during administration?
options: Administer the medication rapidly to achieve higher peak levels
Ensure adequate hydration and monitor urine output and renal function
Mix acyclovir with dopamine in the same intravenous line
Restrict fluids to prevent fluid overload
questions.explanation: Acyclovir can precipitate in the renal tubules and cause crystalline nephropathy, especially with rapid infusion or inadequate hydration. Slow infusion and maintaining good urine output are standard protective measures. Compatibility with other drugs must be checked; fluid restriction increases renal risk.

questions.q: A client under general anesthesia develops sudden hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, and rising end-tidal CO₂. Which medication should the nurse anticipate administering?
options: Naloxone
Dantrolene
Flumazenil
Protamine sulfate
questions.explanation: These signs indicate malignant hyperthermia, a rare but life-threatening hypermetabolic crisis triggered by certain anesthetics and succinylcholine. Dantrolene is the specific antidote; it inhibits calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Immediate discontinuation of triggering agents, hyperventilation with 100% oxygen, cooling, and supportive care are also required.

questions.q: A client receives a large dose of lidocaine for regional anesthesia and develops perioral numbness, tinnitus, and agitation, progressing to seizures. What is the priority nursing action?
options: Administer a benzodiazepine and prepare for lipid emulsion therapy if available
Give a rapid fluid bolus and continue the procedure
Administer epinephrine immediately
Apply oxygen only and observe
questions.explanation: These symptoms suggest local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST). Initial management includes airway support, seizure control (preferably with benzodiazepines), and administration of intravenous lipid emulsion (20% lipid emulsion) according to current ASRA guidelines. Epinephrine is used cautiously and in reduced doses if cardiac arrest occurs.

questions.q: A client with multiple sclerosis is prescribed baclofen. Which teaching point is essential?
options: “Stop the medication abruptly if you feel better.”
“Do not stop this medication suddenly; abrupt withdrawal can cause seizures or hallucinations.”
“This medication has no sedative effects.”
“Alcohol can be safely consumed in normal amounts while taking baclofen.”
questions.explanation: Abrupt discontinuation of baclofen (especially intrathecal, but also oral with chronic use) can precipitate a withdrawal syndrome that includes seizures, hallucinations, rebound spasticity, and in severe cases rhabdomyolysis or multi-organ failure. Gradual tapering is required. Sedation is common, and alcohol potentiates CNS depression.

questions.q: A client with epilepsy and migraines is prescribed topiramate. Which adverse effect should the nurse emphasize in teaching?
options: Significant weight gain and improved appetite
Risk of kidney stones, cognitive slowing, and decreased sweating
Marked hypertension requiring additional medication
Elevation of serum sodium requiring restriction
questions.explanation: Topiramate is associated with nephrolithiasis (encourage hydration), cognitive side effects (“brain fog”), word-finding difficulty, and oligohidrosis/hyperthermia (especially in children). It commonly causes weight loss rather than gain and can cause metabolic acidosis. Clients should be taught to maintain adequate fluid intake and report visual or cognitive changes.

questions.q: A client is scheduled to receive the varicella (chickenpox) vaccine. Which condition is a contraindication to administration?
options: Mild upper respiratory infection without fever
Current pregnancy or planned pregnancy within 1 month
History of penicillin allergy
Stable, well-controlled diabetes
questions.explanation: The varicella vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy because of theoretical risk to the fetus. Women should avoid pregnancy for at least 1 month after vaccination. Mild illnesses without fever are not contraindications; penicillin allergy and stable diabetes are not absolute contraindications for this vaccine.

questions.q: A client with neuropathic pain is prescribed gabapentin. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I should not stop this medication suddenly.”
“This medication may cause drowsiness and dizziness, especially when I first start it.”
“I can double the dose if my pain is not controlled after the first day.”
“I need to be careful when driving until I know how the medication affects me.”
questions.explanation: Gabapentin requires gradual titration to improve tolerability and reduce side effects. Clients should not double doses independently. Abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal symptoms or seizures (in clients with epilepsy). Sedation and dizziness are common, particularly early in therapy, so caution with driving and operating machinery is appropriate.

questions.q: A client receiving haloperidol develops high fever, muscle rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability. What is the nurse’s priority action?
options: Administer the next scheduled dose of haloperidol
Hold the antipsychotic, initiate cooling measures, and notify the provider immediately
Administer a PRN benzodiazepine and reassess in 30 minutes
Encourage oral fluids and monitor vital signs every 4 hours
questions.explanation: These findings are classic for neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), a rare but life-threatening reaction to antipsychotics. Immediate discontinuation of the offending agent, supportive care (including temperature control), and urgent medical notification are required. NMS is a medical emergency; delaying action or continuing the antipsychotic increases morbidity and mortality risk.

questions.q: A client prescribed metoclopramide for gastroparesis develops new restlessness, involuntary muscle movements, and facial grimacing. What should the nurse do first?
options: Document the findings as expected anticholinergic effects
Hold the medication and notify the provider of possible extrapyramidal symptoms
Administer the next dose with food to reduce side effects
Encourage the client to ambulate to relieve restlessness
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist and can cause extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS), including acute dystonia, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia (especially with prolonged use). New-onset involuntary movements require holding the drug and provider notification. Anticholinergic effects are different; continued administration can worsen EPS.

questions.q: A client with acute gout is prescribed colchicine. Which teaching point is most important?
options: “Take the medication only when pain is severe to avoid side effects.”
“Stop the medication and report severe diarrhea, vomiting, or abdominal pain immediately.”
“This medication is safe for long-term daily use at high doses.”
“Colchicine has no interactions with other common medications.”
questions.explanation: Colchicine has a narrow therapeutic index. Gastrointestinal toxicity (severe diarrhea, nausea, vomiting) is an early sign of toxicity and requires immediate discontinuation. High-dose or prolonged regimens increase risk of bone marrow suppression and multiorgan toxicity. Clients should use the lowest effective dose and be aware of significant drug interactions (e.g., with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors).

questions.q: A client with rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus is prescribed hydroxychloroquine. Which monitoring parameter is essential?
options: Serum potassium weekly
Baseline and periodic ophthalmologic examinations
Fasting blood glucose every 3 months only
Complete blood count every 2 days
questions.explanation: Long-term hydroxychloroquine use carries a risk of irreversible retinopathy. Guidelines recommend baseline eye examination and regular ophthalmologic screening (typically annually after 5 years, or earlier with risk factors). Clients should report any visual changes promptly. Other laboratory monitoring may be indicated but is secondary to retinal toxicity surveillance.

questions.q: A client receiving amphotericin B for a systemic fungal infection develops fever, chills, and rigors during the infusion. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
options: Stop the infusion permanently and notify the provider that the client is allergic
Slow or temporarily interrupt the infusion and administer prescribed premedications (e.g., acetaminophen, diphenhydramine)
Increase the infusion rate to complete the dose more quickly
Switch the client to oral fluconazole without consulting the provider
questions.explanation: Amphotericin B commonly causes infusion-related reactions (fever, chills, rigors). Standard management includes premedication and slowing or briefly interrupting the infusion. True hypersensitivity is less common. The infusion should not be accelerated, and antifungal therapy changes require provider orders. Nephrotoxicity and electrolyte wasting are additional major concerns requiring monitoring.

questions.q: A client receiving cisplatin for ovarian cancer is scheduled for the next dose. Which assessment finding requires the nurse to hold the medication and notify the provider?
options: Mild nausea controlled with antiemetics
Urine output of 20 mL/hour despite hydration and serum creatinine elevated from baseline
Alopecia and fatigue
Hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL
questions.explanation: Cisplatin is highly nephrotoxic. Adequate hydration and monitoring of urine output and renal function are mandatory. Oliguria and rising creatinine indicate acute kidney injury and require holding the dose. Nausea, alopecia, and mild anemia are expected or common effects that do not automatically contraindicate administration.

questions.q: A client with supraventricular tachycardia is prescribed intravenous adenosine. Which nursing action is essential during administration?
options: Administer the medication slowly over 5 minutes while monitoring blood pressure
Give the medication as a rapid IV bolus followed by a saline flush, with continuous cardiac monitoring
Dilute the adenosine in 100 mL of fluid and infuse over 30 minutes
Administer only if the client has a history of asthma or COPD
questions.explanation: Adenosine has an extremely short half-life and must be given as a rapid intravenous bolus (typically over 1–2 seconds) followed immediately by a saline flush to ensure it reaches the heart. Continuous cardiac monitoring is required because transient asystole or bradycardia is expected. Slow infusion renders the drug ineffective. It is used cautiously in clients with reactive airway disease.

questions.q: A client develops symptomatic bradycardia with hypotension. Which medication should the nurse anticipate administering first according to standard protocols?
options: Amiodarone
Atropine
Lidocaine
Adenosine
questions.explanation: Atropine is the first-line medication for symptomatic bradycardia in current advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) guidelines. It blocks vagal effects and increases heart rate. Amiodarone and lidocaine are used for certain ventricular arrhythmias; adenosine is used for supraventricular tachycardia. Non-pharmacologic measures (e.g., pacing) may follow if atropine is ineffective.

questions.q: A client prescribed linezolid for vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus is also taking sertraline. What is the nurse’s primary concern?
options: Reduced antibiotic efficacy
Risk of serotonin syndrome
Severe hypotension
Marked hyperglycemia
questions.explanation: Linezolid is a weak monoamine oxidase inhibitor and can interact with serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol, etc.) to precipitate serotonin syndrome. Clients should be monitored for agitation, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, and neuromuscular abnormalities. Dietary tyramine restrictions may also apply with prolonged use. Coordination with the provider regarding the serotonergic medication is essential.

questions.q: A client in the intensive care unit is receiving a continuous propofol infusion for sedation. Which monitoring parameter is the highest priority?
options: Serum triglycerides and signs of propofol-related infusion syndrome (PRIS)
Serum sodium every 12 hours only
Daily weights exclusively
Capillary blood glucose every 6 hours without other assessments
questions.explanation: Prolonged or high-dose propofol infusions can cause propofol-related infusion syndrome (PRIS), characterized by metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, hepatomegaly, renal failure, and cardiovascular collapse. Monitoring of triglycerides, acid-base status, creatine kinase, and clinical signs is essential. Propofol is also formulated in a lipid emulsion, so triglyceride monitoring is routinely recommended.

questions.q: A client with active pulmonary tuberculosis is prescribed isoniazid and rifampin. Which teaching point is most important?
options: “You may stop the medications once your cough improves.”
“Report any yellowing of the skin or eyes, unusual fatigue, or dark urine promptly.”
“These medications have no effect on the color of your body fluids.”
“It is safe to drink alcohol in moderation while taking these drugs.”
questions.explanation: Both isoniazid and rifampin can cause hepatotoxicity. Clients must be taught to recognize and report signs of liver injury immediately. Rifampin commonly causes orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat, and tears (harmless but expected). Therapy requires completion of the full course; alcohol increases hepatotoxicity risk and should be avoided.

questions.q: A client with type 2 diabetes is prescribed glipizide. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I should carry a source of fast-acting carbohydrate with me.”
“This medication can cause low blood sugar, especially if I skip meals.”
“I can safely take this medication if I am allergic to sulfa drugs.”
“I need to monitor my blood glucose regularly while on this drug.”
questions.explanation: Sulfonylureas such as glipizide are sulfonamide derivatives and are contraindicated or used with extreme caution in clients with sulfonamide allergy due to potential cross-reactivity. They stimulate insulin release and carry a significant risk of hypoglycemia, particularly with missed meals or increased activity. Clients must be educated about hypoglycemia recognition, treatment, and regular glucose monitoring.

questions.q: A client with type 2 diabetes is started on empagliflozin. Which adverse effect should the nurse emphasize in teaching?
options: Significant risk of severe hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy
Increased risk of genital mycotic infections and urinary tract infections
Marked weight gain within the first month
Elevation of blood pressure requiring additional antihypertensive therapy
questions.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors increase urinary glucose excretion, which predisposes clients to genital yeast infections and UTIs. They carry a low risk of hypoglycemia when used alone (higher when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas). They typically promote modest weight loss and can lower blood pressure. Clients should also be taught about the rare risk of euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis and the need to stay hydrated.

questions.q: A client prescribed phenelzine (an MAOI) for depression is reviewing dietary restrictions. Which food must the client avoid?
options: Fresh cottage cheese and milk
Aged cheeses, cured meats, and red wine
Fresh fruits such as apples and bananas
Cooked vegetables and lean poultry
questions.explanation: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors prevent the breakdown of tyramine. Ingestion of high-tyramine foods (aged cheeses, cured or smoked meats, fermented products, red wine, certain soy products) can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. Fresh dairy, most fresh fruits (in moderation), and properly cooked fresh foods are generally acceptable. Clients require thorough dietary education and a list of restricted foods.

questions.q: A client with bipolar disorder and seizures is prescribed valproic acid. Which laboratory monitoring is essential?
options: Serum sodium only
Liver function tests and serum valproate levels
Fasting lipid panel every 2 weeks
Arterial blood gases monthly
questions.explanation: Valproic acid can cause hepatotoxicity (including rare fatal hepatic failure) and has a therapeutic range that guides dosing. Baseline and periodic liver function tests, along with serum drug levels, are recommended. Clients should report abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or jaundice promptly. Pancreatitis is another serious adverse effect that requires monitoring of clinical symptoms.

questions.q: A client started on lamotrigine for bipolar disorder develops a widespread rash 10 days after beginning therapy. What is the nurse’s priority action?
options: Apply a topical corticosteroid and continue the medication
Hold the medication and notify the provider immediately
Administer a PRN antihistamine and reassess in 4 hours
Reassure the client that mild rashes are common and self-limiting
questions.explanation: Lamotrigine is associated with serious skin reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, particularly when titrated too rapidly or combined with valproate. Any rash requires immediate evaluation and usually discontinuation of the drug. Early recognition and stopping the medication are critical to prevent progression to life-threatening reactions.

questions.q: A client with osteoarthritis is prescribed long-term ibuprofen. Which teaching point is most important?
options: “Take this medication on an empty stomach for faster relief.”
“Report any black, tarry stools, coffee-ground emesis, or unusual bruising.”
“This medication has no effect on kidney function.”
“You may safely take higher doses than prescribed if pain is severe.”
questions.explanation: NSAIDs increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding and ulceration. Clients must be taught to recognize and report signs of GI bleeding. NSAIDs can also cause renal impairment, fluid retention, and elevated blood pressure; they should be taken with food and at the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration. Exceeding prescribed doses increases toxicity risk.

questions.q: A client is brought to the emergency department after ingesting a large amount of acetaminophen 6 hours earlier. Which medication should the nurse anticipate administering?
options: Naloxone
N-acetylcysteine
Flumazenil
Protamine sulfate
questions.explanation: N-acetylcysteine is the specific antidote for acetaminophen overdose and is most effective when given within 8–12 hours of ingestion (though still beneficial later). It replenishes glutathione and prevents hepatotoxicity. Naloxone reverses opioids, flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, and protamine reverses heparin. Serum acetaminophen levels and liver function tests guide management according to established protocols (e.g., Rumack-Matthew nomogram).

questions.q: A 5-year-old child is recovering from a viral illness. The parent asks about giving aspirin for fever. What is the most appropriate nursing response?
options: “Aspirin is the preferred antipyretic for children.”
“Aspirin should be avoided in children with viral illnesses because of the risk of Reye syndrome.”
“You may give aspirin if the fever is higher than 39°C (102.2°F).”
“Aspirin is safe as long as the child has not received the influenza vaccine.”
questions.explanation: Aspirin use in children and adolescents with viral infections (especially influenza or varicella) is associated with Reye syndrome, a rare but serious condition causing hepatic encephalopathy. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen (if appropriate) are preferred antipyretics in this age group. This warning is a longstanding public health and pediatric guideline recommendation.

questions.q: A client has been taking high-dose prednisone for 6 weeks for an autoimmune flare. The provider plans to discontinue the medication. Which action is essential?
options: Stop the prednisone abruptly to minimize total steroid exposure
Taper the dose gradually according to a prescribed schedule
Switch immediately to an equipotent dose of dexamethasone without tapering
Discontinue the steroid and start high-dose NSAIDs to prevent rebound
questions.explanation: Prolonged systemic corticosteroid use suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. Abrupt discontinuation can precipitate adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis). Standard practice is to taper the dose gradually to allow recovery of endogenous cortisol production. The taper schedule is individualized based on dose, duration, and clinical status.

questions.q: A client who received a kidney transplant is prescribed tacrolimus. Which laboratory value is the highest priority for the nurse to monitor?
options: Serum sodium
Tacrolimus trough level and serum creatinine
Fasting blood glucose only after 3 months
Complete blood count every 2 days indefinitely
questions.explanation: Tacrolimus has a narrow therapeutic index; trough levels are used to guide dosing and avoid toxicity or rejection. Nephrotoxicity is a major adverse effect, so concurrent monitoring of serum creatinine (and other renal parameters) is essential. Hyperglycemia can occur but is not the immediate priority parameter; routine frequent CBCs are more critical for other agents such as clozapine or certain antimetabolites.

questions.q: A client receiving doxorubicin for breast cancer reports new onset of fatigue, dyspnea, and mild ankle edema. What is the nurse’s priority action?
options: Reassure the client that these symptoms are expected with chemotherapy
Notify the provider and prepare for cardiac evaluation (e.g., echocardiogram)
Administer a PRN diuretic and reassess in 4 hours
Encourage increased oral fluid intake to improve energy
questions.explanation: Doxorubicin is associated with cumulative, dose-dependent cardiotoxicity that can lead to cardiomyopathy and heart failure. New or worsening cardiac symptoms require prompt evaluation of cardiac function. Standard oncology guidelines emphasize monitoring cumulative dose and assessing for early signs of cardiac toxicity rather than attributing symptoms solely to general chemotherapy effects.

questions.q: A client receiving vincristine develops new numbness and tingling in the fingers and toes. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Document the finding as an expected side effect and continue the infusion
Hold the medication and notify the provider of possible peripheral neuropathy
Apply warm compresses to the extremities and reassess in 1 hour
Administer a PRN analgesic and encourage ambulation
questions.explanation: Vincristine commonly causes dose-limiting peripheral neuropathy. New or progressive sensory changes require prompt reporting because continued administration can lead to severe, potentially irreversible neuropathy or motor impairment. Vincristine is also a vesicant; however, the  focuses on neuropathy. Holding and notifying allows for possible dose adjustment or supportive measures per oncology protocols.

questions.q: A client with hyperthyroidism is prescribed methimazole. Which teaching point is most important?
options: “Report any sore throat, fever, or unusual bruising immediately.”
“This medication can be stopped once your heart rate normalizes.”
“Take the medication only when you feel symptoms of hyperthyroidism.”
“Methimazole has no effect on white blood cell count.”
questions.explanation: Methimazole (and propylthiouracil) can cause agranulocytosis, a rare but life-threatening adverse effect. Clients must be taught to report signs of infection (sore throat, fever) or bleeding/bruising promptly so that a complete blood count can be checked. Therapy is usually continued until the client is euthyroid and often longer; it is not taken only for breakthrough symptoms.

questions.q: A client with acute diarrhea is prescribed loperamide. In which situation should the nurse  the order?
options: Client with traveler’s diarrhea and no fever
Client with bloody stools and high fever suggestive of invasive bacterial infection
Client with mild viral gastroenteritis
Client requesting medication for frequent loose stools after chemotherapy
questions.explanation: Antimotility agents such as loperamide are contraindicated in clients with suspected invasive bacterial enteritis (bloody diarrhea, high fever) because slowing gut motility can prolong toxin exposure and worsen outcomes (e.g., risk of toxic megacolon). They may be appropriate for non-invasive diarrhea once infectious causes are excluded or in selected other situations under guidance.

questions.q: A client is prescribed bisacodyl for constipation. Which instruction is appropriate?
options: “Crush the enteric-coated tablet and mix it with juice for easier swallowing.”
“Take the tablet with a full glass of water and do not chew or crush it.”
“This medication is safe for daily long-term use without risk of dependence.”
“Expect a bowel movement within 5–10 minutes of taking the oral tablet.”
questions.explanation: Enteric-coated bisacodyl tablets must be swallowed whole; crushing or chewing can cause gastric irritation and reduce effectiveness. Oral bisacodyl typically produces a bowel movement in 6–12 hours. Stimulant laxatives are generally recommended for short-term use because prolonged daily use can lead to dependence and electrolyte imbalance.

questions.q: A client is prescribed varenicline for smoking cessation. Which client report requires immediate follow-up?
options: Vivid dreams during the first week
New or worsening depressed mood and suicidal thoughts
Mild nausea after doses
Temporary increase in appetite
questions.explanation: Varenicline has been associated with neuropsychiatric effects, including changes in mood, behavior, and suicidal ideation. Clients must be monitored and taught to report any new or worsening depression, agitation, or suicidal thoughts immediately. Vivid dreams and nausea are common and often improve; appetite changes can occur but are less urgent.

questions.q: A nurse is preparing to administer intravenous potassium chloride 10 mEq in 100 mL of normal saline. Which action is essential for safe administration?
options: Administer the solution by IV push over 1–2 minutes
Infuse via a calibrated pump at a rate not exceeding institutional limits (commonly ≤10 mEq/hour peripherally)
Add the potassium to a hanging IV bag without mixing
Give the potassium through the same line as a continuous insulin infusion without flushing
questions.explanation: Intravenous potassium is a high-alert medication. It must never be given by IV push and should be infused slowly via a pump, typically at no more than 10 mEq/hour through a peripheral line (higher rates require central access and continuous cardiac monitoring). Proper dilution and thorough mixing are required. Concurrent administration with insulin requires careful line management to avoid unintended effects.

questions.q: A client with bipolar disorder and trigeminal neuralgia is prescribed carbamazepine. Which laboratory monitoring is essential?
options: Serum sodium and complete blood count
Fasting lipid panel monthly
Serum calcium weekly
Arterial blood gases daily
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine can cause hyponatremia (SIADH) and bone marrow suppression (including rare aplastic anemia or agranulocytosis). Baseline and periodic monitoring of serum sodium and CBC is recommended. Clients should also be taught to report fever, sore throat, or unusual bleeding. Lipid and calcium monitoring are not primary requirements for this agent.

questions.q: A client with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is started on clozapine. Which monitoring parameter is the highest priority?
options: Weekly complete blood count with absolute neutrophil count for the first 6 months
Serum lithium level every 3 months
Fasting blood glucose only after 1 year
Liver function tests every 2 weeks indefinitely
questions.explanation: Clozapine carries a significant risk of agranulocytosis. Strict monitoring of absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is mandatory—typically weekly for the first 6 months, then every 2 weeks, then monthly—per national registries and prescribing guidelines. Therapy is interrupted if ANC falls below defined thresholds. Metabolic monitoring is also important but secondary to the life-threatening hematologic risk in the early phase.

questions.q: A client with non-valvular atrial fibrillation is prescribed apixaban. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding of the medication?
options: “I will need regular blood tests to check my INR while taking this drug.”
“I should not stop this medication suddenly without talking to my provider, even if I feel fine.”
“If I miss a dose, I should double the next dose to catch up.”
“This medication is reversed with vitamin K if I have bleeding.”
questions.explanation: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) such as apixaban do not require routine INR monitoring. Abrupt discontinuation increases the risk of thrombotic events; clients must consult the provider before stopping. Missed doses should not be doubled. The specific reversal agent for apixaban is andexanet alfa (not vitamin K, which is used for warfarin). These points align with current anticoagulation guidelines.

questions.q: A client receiving intravenous amiodarone for atrial fibrillation develops a new cough, low-grade fever, and dyspnea. What is the nurse’s priority action?
options: Reassure the client that these are expected side effects
Notify the provider and prepare for possible chest imaging
Administer a PRN bronchodilator and reassess in 1 hour
Increase the infusion rate to achieve faster rhythm control
questions.explanation: Amiodarone carries a risk of pulmonary toxicity (pneumonitis or fibrosis) that can present with cough, fever, and dyspnea. Early recognition and discontinuation are critical because toxicity can be irreversible. Standard monitoring guidelines require prompt evaluation (including imaging and pulmonary function assessment) rather than assuming the symptoms are benign or treating symptomatically without provider notification.

questions.q: A client with heart failure is prescribed spironolactone. Which laboratory value requires the nurse to hold the dose and contact the provider?
options: Serum potassium 5.7 mEq/L
Serum sodium 136 mEq/L
Blood pressure 128/78 mm Hg
Serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL
questions.explanation: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic (aldosterone antagonist). Hyperkalemia is a significant adverse effect, especially when combined with ACE inhibitors/ARBs or in renal impairment. A potassium of 5.7 mEq/L exceeds safe limits and warrants holding the medication and notifying the provider. The other values are within acceptable ranges and do not require immediate action.

questions.q: A client is prescribed azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia. Which concurrent medication would cause the nurse to  the order?
options: Acetaminophen for fever
A medication known to prolong the QT interval
An inhaled corticosteroid
A multivitamin without minerals
questions.explanation: Macrolides such as azithromycin can prolong the QT interval and increase the risk of torsades de pointes, particularly when combined with other QT-prolonging drugs or in clients with pre-existing risk factors. Guidelines recommend caution or avoidance of such combinations. The other listed agents do not pose the same significant interaction risk.

questions.q: A client with a systemic fungal infection is started on fluconazole. Which laboratory parameter should be monitored regularly?
options: Serum potassium only
Liver function tests
Fasting blood glucose
Complete blood count every 2 days
questions.explanation: Fluconazole (and other azole antifungals) can cause hepatotoxicity. Baseline and periodic liver function tests are recommended, especially with prolonged therapy or higher doses. While drug interactions and other effects exist, hepatic monitoring is a primary safety parameter in clinical guidelines. Frequent CBC monitoring is more characteristic of other agents (e.g., flucytosine or certain chemotherapy).

questions.q: A client with confirmed influenza is prescribed oseltamivir. When is this medication most effective?
options: When started within 48 hours of symptom onset
Only after symptoms have been present for at least 5 days
As long-term prophylaxis for the entire flu season without regard to exposure
After the client has already received the influenza vaccine that season
questions.explanation: Neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir are most effective at reducing symptom duration and complications when initiated within 48 hours of influenza symptom onset. They may still be considered later in severe or high-risk cases, but early treatment provides the greatest benefit according to public health and infectious disease guidelines. Vaccination status does not preclude treatment.

questions.q: A client experiencing anaphylaxis is prescribed intramuscular epinephrine. Which site is preferred for administration in an adult?
options: Deltoid muscle
Vastus lateralis (anterolateral thigh)
Gluteal muscle
Subcutaneous tissue of the abdomen
questions.explanation: Current anaphylaxis guidelines (e.g., from allergy and emergency medicine organizations) recommend the anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis) as the preferred site for intramuscular epinephrine because it provides the most rapid and reliable absorption. The deltoid may be used if the thigh is inaccessible, but the thigh is first-line. Subcutaneous administration is slower and not preferred for anaphylaxis; the gluteal site is avoided due to variable absorption and sciatic nerve risk.

questions.q: A client is prescribed a combined oral contraceptive. Which client condition is an absolute contraindication to its use?
options: History of migraine without aura
Current tobacco use and age greater than 35 years
Mild hypertension controlled with one medication
Family history of breast cancer in a second-degree relative
questions.explanation: Combined hormonal contraceptives are contraindicated in women older than 35 years who smoke (especially ≥15 cigarettes per day) because of significantly elevated risk of cardiovascular events (stroke, myocardial infarction). This is a CDC Medical Eligibility Criteria Category 4 (unacceptable health risk). The other conditions may require caution or alternative methods but are not absolute contraindications in the same way.

questions.q: A client in labor is receiving intravenous oxytocin for augmentation. Which finding requires the nurse to stop the infusion immediately?
options: Contractions occurring every 3 minutes and lasting 50 seconds
Fetal heart rate with moderate variability and accelerations
Contractions lasting longer than 90 seconds or occurring more frequently than every 2 minutes
Maternal blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg
questions.explanation: Uterine tachysystole (contractions lasting >90 seconds or more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes) increases risk of fetal hypoxia and uterine rupture. Standard obstetric protocols require immediate discontinuation of oxytocin, maternal repositioning, oxygen if needed, and notification of the provider. Normal contraction frequency/duration and reassuring fetal heart rate tracings do not require stopping the infusion.

questions.q: An 82-year-old client is prescribed a new medication with significant anticholinergic effects. Which adverse effect is the nurse most concerned about in this age group?
options: Mild dry mouth
Confusion, urinary retention, and increased fall risk
Temporary improvement in memory
Decreased appetite only
